name: Survodutide

lead: Survodutide is a weekly injection that activates glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. It is in phase 3 trials for obesity and liver disease, from Boehringer Ingelheim.
Phase 2 and 3 trials report weight loss in people with obesity, but it is not approved and has no cosmetic-use evidence.

paras: GLP-1 activation reduces appetite while glucagon receptor activation is thought to raise energy expenditure and act on the liver.

Safety is still under evaluation in phase 3 and cardiovascular outcomes trials. As a GLP-1-class drug, questions include muscle, bone and gastrointestinal effects. It is not available as an approved medicine.

lead: Survodutide (BI 456906) is an investigational once-weekly injectable peptide that activates both the glucagon receptor and the GLP-1 receptor. It is being developed by Boehringer Ingelheim for obesity, type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and has not been approved as a medicine at the time of writing. [1][2][3][4]

Its logic is that adding glucagon-receptor activation, which is thought to raise energy expenditure and act on the liver, may produce more weight loss than GLP-1 receptor agonism alone. [1][5] Reviews group it with retatrutide and mazdutide among glucagon/GLP-1 co-agonists. [1][5]

Phase 2 trials have reported weight loss and liver benefits, and phase 3 results in obesity and in obesity with fatty liver disease were published in 2026. [6][7][8][9] No community discussion of it for appearance was available for this entry, and the evidence relates to medical weight management in people with obesity rather than cosmetic use.
infobox: Dual glucagon receptor / GLP-1 receptor agonist

paras: Survodutide is under study for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, and for MASH and MASLD. [6][8][9][10][11] Registered phase 3 trials include the SYNCHRONIZE programme in obesity, a study in adults with cirrhosis due to MASH, studies in type 2 diabetes, and a study in women through or after menopause. [12][13][14][15]
Obesity (phase 2): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding trial at 43 centres in 12 countries examined safety, tolerability and efficacy of survodutide for obesity. [7]

Obesity (phase 3): a phase 3 trial of once-weekly survodutide in adults with obesity was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2026, and SYNCHRONIZE-MASLD, in adults with obesity and fatty liver disease, was published in Nature Medicine the same year. [8][9] The design of the two phase 3 obesity trials and a cardiovascular outcomes trial has been described. [10][11]

MASH: a 48-week phase 2 trial in adults with biopsy-confirmed MASH and fibrosis stages F1 to F3 tested survodutide against placebo, and a phase 1 study examined it in cirrhosis. [6][16] Reviews and a network meta-analysis include survodutide among agents showing promise for MASH resolution and fibrosis. [17][18]
Type 2 diabetes: a phase 2 trial compared several doses with placebo and open-label semaglutide for HbA1c and bodyweight. [19]
These trials involve patients with obesity or liver disease. No studies found of survodutide in healthy people seeking an aesthetic change.

Safety is being assessed across the trials above, including cardiovascular outcomes and tolerability. A review of GLP-1-based medicines discusses safety questions for the class, including effects on muscle strength, bone density, gastrointestinal motility and retained gastric contents. [1] Another review notes that glucagon co-agonists such as survodutide have shown significant weight loss and glycaemic improvement. [5]

Ongoing registered studies include a phase 3 trial for people with obesity without diabetes, a trial on heart structure and function in obesity with fatty liver disease, formulation comparisons for pre-filled syringes and pen injectors, and a study of energy use and fat breakdown. [20][21][22][23] Systematic reviews of emerging obesity drugs list survodutide among phase 3 GLP-1/glucagon co-agonists. [2]

timeline.event: Phase 2 trials in obesity, MASH and type 2 diabetes are published. [6][7][19]
